newsitem.title: USA: Jury selected in South American bank case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selected in South American bank case.

text.p: A retired union member, two nurses, an actor and an unemployed parking attendant were among 12 jurors selected on Wednesday to hear a complex bank fraud case against a Cuban-born banker, his son and grandson.

The three are accused of illegally using deposits in a family-controlled bank, Banco Progreso International de Puerto Rico (BPIPR), to prop up financial institutions they controlled in Central and South America.
The case is being tried in New York because prosecutors claim money in the alleged fraud was transferred through New York banks, including two multimillion dollar transfers.

Orlandi Castro Llanes, known as "Don Orlando", his son Orlando Castro Castro and grandson Jorge Castro Barredo Castro, are charged with scheming to defraud. The two younger men also face grand larceny charges. All three men have pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The jurors, six men and six women and six alternates were to be sworn in on Thursday by Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Edward McLaughlin before the start of opening statements by prosecutors and defence lawyers.

In the jury selection process that began on Nov. 12, both prosecution and defence attorneys excluded prospective jurors who either worked or had friends in banking, brokerage houses or were familiar with international banking.

U.S. prosecutors claim the three bankers misled Venezuelan depositors to believe BPIPR was a safe off-shore bank subject to tight regulatory control, attracting deposits of more than $55 million. They said BPIPR closed down in January 1995 with uninsured loses to depositors of more than $15 million.

Castro, a Cuban exile accused of playing a key role in Venezuela's 1994 banking crisis, left Venezuela that year after arrest warrants were issued for him and several associates on charges of financial fraud and other crimes.
All three men have been in jail since they were arrested in April. The Venezuelan government has begun extradition proceedings.
